mcqs.question: A camera preview should only run while the Activity is actually in the foreground and interactive, pausing the instant a dialog appears over it. Which lifecycle pair should start and stop it?
options: onCreate / onDestroy
onResume / onPause
onStart / onStop
onAttach / onDetach
mcqs.explanation: onResume/onPause bracket interactivity specifically — a dialog appearing over the Activity triggers onPause even though the Activity is still visible, which is exactly the boundary needed for something like a camera preview that must stop the instant focus is lost, not just when visibility changes.

mcqs.question: Why does rotating the device destroy and recreate the Activity by default, rather than just re-laying-out the existing views?
options: Rotation is treated as a configuration change, and Android's default response to any configuration change is to tear down and rebuild the Activity so every configuration-dependent resource is re-read from scratch
Rotation always crashes the app unless explicitly handled
Recreating the Activity is required by the Android OS for battery-saving reasons
Only Fragments are destroyed on rotation; Activities are unaffected
mcqs.explanation: Resources like layout XML and strings can vary by configuration (orientation, locale), so rather than building selective re-fetching logic, Android destroys and recreates the whole Activity on any configuration change to guarantee every resource is correctly re-resolved — this applies to the Activity itself, not just its Fragments.

mcqs.question: A Fragment holds a reference to one of its views in a class field, and the app crashes with a reference to a destroyed view shortly after the Fragment is pushed onto the back stack. What's the most likely cause?
options: The Fragment's view was destroyed via onDestroyView while the Fragment object itself remained alive, but the field holding the view reference was never nulled out
Fragments cannot be placed on the back stack at all
The Activity itself was destroyed, taking the Fragment down with it
The view field should have been declared static instead
mcqs.explanation: A Fragment going onto the back stack triggers onDestroyView while the Fragment object itself survives — a view reference held in a field that isn't cleared in onDestroyView becomes stale, and any later use of it after the view is gone is exactly this bug. Nulling out view references in onDestroyView is the standard fix.

mcqs.question: A screen holds a large in-memory list fetched from the network, and needs it to survive a rotation without re-fetching, but doesn't need it to survive an actual process death. What's the appropriate mechanism?
options: onSaveInstanceState with the list serialized into the Bundle
A static field on the Activity class
ViewModel, which is retained across the Activity's destroy/recreate cycle for a configuration change without needing to survive full process death
SharedPreferences
mcqs.explanation: ViewModel is specifically retained across a configuration-change-triggered recreation, making it a natural fit for exactly this need, without the size and process-death-persistence tradeoffs of a Bundle, which is meant for small primitives, not large in-memory objects.

mcqs.question: A utility class stores the current Activity in a static field to avoid passing Context around. What's the resulting risk?
options: The static reference prevents the garbage collector from reclaiming the Activity and everything it holds, even after the Activity is destroyed, leaking memory across every rotation or navigation that recreates it
The app will crash immediately the first time the Activity is destroyed
The static field will automatically be cleared by the OS on Activity destruction
This only causes a problem if the Activity is a singleton itself
mcqs.explanation: A static field's lifetime spans the whole app process, so an Activity reference stored there outlives the Activity's own destruction and prevents garbage collection of its entire object graph — a slow, cumulative leak across rotations rather than an immediate crash, which is exactly why it's easy to miss during quick testing.

mcqs.question: A synchronous, blocking file read runs inside onCreate. Why is this worse on Android than it might initially seem?
options: It only affects the very first app launch, never subsequent screens
This is only a problem if the file being read is larger than 1MB
onCreate runs on a background thread by default, so blocking work there has no visible effect
It delays the first frame on every single Activity creation, including every rotation-triggered recreation, and its impact is disproportionately worse on lower-end devices than on a fast dev device
mcqs.explanation: onCreate runs on the main thread and gates the first visible frame, and because rotation re-triggers onCreate, the same blocking cost repeats on every rotation, not just app launch — the effect is also magnified on slower devices with cold caches, which a fast dev device won't reveal.
